entries.label: A radius that stops short of the circle
entries.description: Starts correctly at the centre but ends anywhere, as though a radius were a direction rather than a fixed length.
entries.signal: One end is the centre; the other is strictly inside the circle.

refutation.text_md: You started in the right place — the centre — which is the part most people get wrong.
But a radius has to REACH the circle. It is not any segment leaving the centre; it is the fixed distance from the centre to the circle.
That fixed distance is what makes it a circle in the first place: every point on the circle is exactly $r$ from $M$.
So a radius always has two jobs: start at $M$, and end ON the circle.

Its definitions are standard: a radius runs from the centre to the circle, and every point on the circle is r from M. entries.label: A radius drawn between two points on the circle
entries.description: Builds a segment with both ends on the circle and calls it a radius — the word is attached to 'a line in the circle' rather than to the centre.
entries.signal: Both endpoints satisfy the circle; neither is the centre.

refutation.text_md: Look at what you drew: both ends landed on the circle, and that is a real thing — it is a chord.
A radius is the one segment that always starts at the centre $M$ and stops at the circle. Its whole job is to carry the circle's fixed distance.
That is why every radius of a circle has the same length, and chords do not: a chord can be short or long, but a radius cannot.
Next time, ask where the segment STARTS. Centre to circle is a radius; circle to circle is a chord.

entries.label: A tangent drawn cutting the circle at two points
entries.description: Reads 'tangent' as any line touching or crossing the circle, missing that it meets it exactly once.
entries.signal: The distance from the centre to the line is less than $r$, so the line is a secant.

refutation.text_md: Your line does meet the circle, so you are close — but it meets it TWICE.
A line that cuts a circle at two points is a secant. A tangent touches at exactly one point and then leaves.
The test is a distance: measure from the centre $M$ to the line. Less than $r$ and it cuts twice; equal to $r$ and it touches once; more than $r$ and it misses.
So a tangent is the line whose distance from the centre is exactly the radius.

entries.label: A tangent drawn missing the circle altogether
entries.description: Reads 'tangent' as a line running alongside the circle without meeting it.

refutation.text_md: Running alongside the circle is the right instinct — a tangent does lie against it.
But it has to TOUCH. Your line stays clear of the circle, so it meets it nowhere at all.
Bring it in until the distance from the centre $M$ equals the radius exactly. That single point of contact is what makes it a tangent.
One number decides it: distance from the centre, compared with $r$.

entries.label: Adds the radii when the circles touch internally
entries.description: The student takes the distance between the centres as the sum of the radii even though the circles touch from inside.
entries.signal: For radii 10 cm and 6 cm touching internally, uses MN = 16 cm and gets a much smaller AB than 12 cm (e.g. 24 = 1/2 × 16 × AB gives AB = 3 cm).

refutation.text_md: You are using $MN = 10 + 6$, which is right when two circles touch from outside. You were right that the point of contact lies on the line of centers, and that is the key fact.

When the circles touch internally, the small circle sits inside the big one. Both centers lie on the same line through $A$, on the same side of $A$. $M$ is 10 cm from $A$ and $N$ is only 6 cm from $A$, so $N$ lies between $M$ and $A$.
So the gap between the centers is what is left of the big radius: $MN = 10 - 6 = 4$ cm. Using 16 would put $N$ beyond $A$, outside the big circle.
The wrong base changes the answer. With $MN = 16$, $24 = \tfrac12 \times 16 \times AB$ gives $AB = 3$ cm. With $MN = 4$, $24 = \tfrac12 \times 4 \times AB$ gives $AB = 12$ cm.
Before you use $MN$, ask whether the circles touch externally (add the radii) or internally (subtract them).

verdict.reason: The error is real and matches the example's "(why?)" step. The refutation's arithmetic is correct: MN = 10 − 6 = 4, so AB = 12 from 24 = ½·4·AB, and MN = 16 gives AB = 3. It matches the canonical method and answer. It argues against the specific mistake of adding radii for internal touching. It cites no question ids, pages or figures, and it contrasts with external touching (add radii), which the book also uses.

entries.label: Thinks two circles through A and B can meet at a third point
entries.description: The student believes that two different circles drawn through the same two points A and B can also cross or touch at more than two points.

refutation.text_md: You are right that many circles pass through both $A$ and $B$, so they all share those two points. The doubt is whether two of them could share a third point as well.
The center of every circle through $A$ and $B$ lies on the axis of the chord $AB$. Different centers on that axis give different circles, and all of them meet at $A$ and $B$.

Suppose a circle also went through a third point $C$. Its center would then lie on the axis of $AB$ and on the axis of the chord $AC$, and those two axes cross in only one point. So there is only one possible center and only one circle.
Two different circles therefore cannot intersect in more than two points. When two circles pass through $A$ and $B$, those two points are all they share.

verdict.reason: The error is plausible and the book's rule says two circles cannot meet in more than two points. The refutation uses only the book's idea that the center lies on the axis of any chord. A third common point C would put the center on both the axis of AB and the axis of AC, and two such distinct axes meet in one point, so the circle would be unique. That is correct and fits the canonical method. It cites no outside references. It leaves out the case where C is collinear with A and B, but then no circle passes through all three points, so this doesn't harm the argument.

entries.label: Takes the distance to a chord as a segment to its endpoint
entries.description: The student treats a segment from the center to an end of the chord (such as a radius) as the chord's distance from the center, instead of the perpendicular segment to the midpoint.

refutation.text_md: You are right that the converse is about distances from the center. The slip is in which segment counts as the distance of a chord from the center.

The distance of a chord from the center is the perpendicular segment from the center to the chord. It meets the chord at its midpoint, like $MX$ where $X$ is the midpoint of the chord. A segment from the center to an endpoint of the chord is a radius, and it is not this distance.

Take a chord $AB = 16$ cm with midpoint $E$ and $ME = 6$ cm. Then $AE = 8$ cm and $AM^2 = 6^2 + 8^2 = 100$, so $AM = 10$ cm. The distance is $6$, not $10$. Every radius in the circle is $10$, so comparing radii would make every chord look equidistant.

Before you use the converse, find the perpendicular from the center to each chord, such as $ME$ and $MF$. If those two are equal, the chords are equal. If you only have a radius or a half-chord, use right-triangle working like the one above to find the perpendicular first.

verdict.reason: The error is plausible and matches the book's remark that a chord's distance from the center is MX, with X the midpoint. Every step is correct: the distance is the perpendicular to the midpoint, a radius is not that distance, and the 16/6/8/10 numbers check (6²+8²=100). It uses only the Pythagorean method the book uses, and it argues against this specific error. It names no question ids, pages or figures.
